name: Pale Charcoal
lede: Pale Charcoal is ColorHub's English name for Sabi-onando, a dark, slightly green-grey blue that the traditional Japanese color list ties to storage chests rather than to ash.

sections.title: A storage-chest grey, not an ember grey
sections.body:
Wikipedia's list of traditional Japanese colors gives this swatch as Sabi-onando (錆御納戸), where sabi means "rust" and onando names a dark blue-grey once used for the cloth lining storage chests (nando) [1]. ColorHub's English rendering, Pale Charcoal, borrows the ember word for a tone that is actually a weathered blue-grey, not a true grey from burnt wood [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 places it in block 156, "dark greenish gray," about 4.5 units from that block's centre [2]. The library's nearest other named colors are [[dark-teal-grey]] and [[dark-teal-grey]], each 2.8 units away [2].

Measured in LCH it reads lightness 36, chroma 8, hue 203 degrees, a cool, muted blue-green [2]. The small chroma value means the color sits close to neutral grey on screen, which is why "charcoal" reads plausibly even though the Japanese name points to rust and storage cloth, not to burnt fuel [1][2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a close match in only 450 of 23,781 paintings, under 2 percent, as photographed [3]. Paul Cézanne's work carries it at nearly 14 times the archive's overall rate, in 13 of his 50 dated paintings [3]. It plays a mid-tone role about half the time and a shadow the rest, rarely a highlight [3]. It shares canvases more than chance with the color word Petrol, at nearly 20 times the ordinary rate, and its presence peaks in the 1930s, in 6 of 69 paintings [3].
